cards.q: What is ionic bonding?
cards.a: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, arranged in a lattice.
cards.why: The attraction acts in all directions, so each ion is attracted to every neighbouring ion of opposite charge, not to one partner.

cards.q: How can you predict the charge on a simple ion from the position of its element in the Periodic Table?
cards.a:
Group 1: 1+, Group 2: 2+, Group 13 (3): 3+.
Group 15 (5): 3−, Group 16 (6): 2−, Group 17 (7): 1−.
cards.why: Metals lose their outer electrons and non-metals gain electrons until each ion has the electron configuration of a noble gas.

cards.q: Give the formulas of the sulfate, hydroxide, nitrate, carbonate and ammonium ions.
cards.a: Sulfate \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\), hydroxide \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), nitrate \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\), carbonate \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}\), ammonium \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\).
cards.why: These compound ions stay together as one unit in a formula and in reactions.

cards.q: Write the formula of aluminium sulfate.
steps: Aluminium is in Group 13, so the ion is \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\). Sulfate is \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\).
The charges must cancel: the lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6.
Two \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) give 6+; three \(\mathrm{SO_{4}^{2-}}\) give 6−.
cards.why: Brackets go round a compound ion when more than one of it is needed.

cards.q: Write the formulas of calcium nitrate and ammonium carbonate.
steps: \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\) needs two \(\mathrm{NO_{3}^{-}}\) ions to balance its charge.
\(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}\) needs two \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) ions to balance its charge.
cards.why: The total positive charge must equal the total negative charge.

cards.q: Describe, in terms of electrons, how magnesium oxide forms from magnesium and oxygen atoms, and how its dot-and-cross diagram is drawn.
cards.a: Each Mg atom transfers two electrons to an O atom, forming \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\).
marks: Mg (2,8,2) loses its two outer electrons to become \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), with configuration 2,8.
O (2,6) gains two electrons to become \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\), with configuration 2,8.
In the diagram the oxide ion’s outer shell shows 6 dots and 2 crosses (the electrons from magnesium); the Mg²⁺ ion is drawn with an empty (or no) outer shell.
Each ion is drawn in square brackets with its charge outside the bracket.

cards.q: Explain why magnesium oxide (melting point about \(2850\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)) has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride (\(801\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)).
cards.a: The ions in MgO have greater charges and are smaller, so the ionic bonding is stronger.
marks: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) carry twice the charge of \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\).
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) is smaller than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) is smaller than \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\), so the ions are closer together.
So the electrostatic attraction between the ions is stronger.
More energy is needed to overcome it, so the melting point is higher.

cards.q: Explain why ionic radius increases down a group, for example from Li⁺ to K⁺ or from F⁻ to I⁻.
cards.a: Each ion further down has an extra occupied shell of electrons.
marks: Going down the group, each ion has one more occupied electron shell.
The outer electrons are further from the nucleus.
The extra shielding and distance outweigh the increase in nuclear charge.

cards.q: Explain the trend in ionic radius across the isoelectronic series \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\), \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\), \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\).
cards.a: The radius decreases from \(\mathrm{N^{3-}}\) (largest) to \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) (smallest).
marks: All the ions have the same number of electrons (10) and the same configuration, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.
The number of protons increases from 7 to 13.
The greater nuclear charge pulls the same number of electrons closer, so the ion is smaller.

cards.q: How do the physical properties of ionic compounds provide evidence that they contain ions?
cards.a: High melting points and electrical conduction only when molten or dissolved both fit a lattice of charged particles.
marks: High melting points: strong electrostatic attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
They do not conduct when solid: the ions are fixed in the lattice.
They conduct when molten or in aqueous solution: the ions are free to move and carry charge.
Many dissolve in polar solvents such as water, whose molecules are attracted to the ions.

cards.q: Green copper(II) chromate solution is placed at the bottom of a U-tube under a colourless electrolyte, with an electrode in each arm, and a d.c. supply is connected. What is seen, and what does it show?
cards.a: A blue colour moves towards the negative electrode and a yellow colour moves towards the positive electrode.
cards.why: Blue \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) ions are attracted to the cathode and yellow \(\mathrm{CrO_{4}^{2-}}\) ions to the anode: the migration of coloured ions is evidence that ions exist.

cards.q: True or false: solid sodium chloride conducts electricity because it is made of ions.
cards.a: False. Solid sodium chloride does not conduct.
cards.why: The ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice. They can move, and carry charge, only when the solid is melted or dissolved.

cards.q: What is a covalent bond?
cards.a: A shared pair of electrons: the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei and the shared pair of electrons between them.
cards.why: Both nuclei are attracted to the same pair of electrons, which holds the two atoms together.

cards.q: How many shared pairs of electrons are in the bonds in \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{O_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{N_{2}}\)?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\): one shared pair (single bond).
\(\mathrm{O_{2}}\): two shared pairs (double bond).
\(\mathrm{N_{2}}\): three shared pairs (triple bond).
cards.why: A multiple bond contains more than one shared pair. A single bond is drawn as one line, a double bond as two lines, a triple bond as three.

cards.q: Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of carbon dioxide, \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\).
cards.a: Carbon in the middle shares two pairs of electrons with each oxygen atom (two double bonds). Each oxygen also has two lone pairs.
cards.why: Every atom then has eight electrons in its outer shell. Carbon has no lone pairs.

cards.q: What is a dative covalent (co-ordinate) bond, and how is it shown in a displayed formula?
cards.a: A shared pair of electrons in which both electrons come from the same atom. It is drawn as an arrow pointing away from the atom that donates the pair.
cards.why: The donor atom must have a lone pair; the acceptor must have an empty orbital in its outer shell.

cards.q: Explain how the ammonium ion, \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\), forms from ammonia, and how its four N–H bonds compare.
cards.a: The lone pair on the nitrogen of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) forms a dative bond to an \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ion: \(\mathrm{NH_{3} + H^{+} \rightarrow NH_{4}^{+}}\).
cards.why: Once formed, the dative bond is identical to the other three N–H bonds: all four have the same length and strength.

cards.q: Which bond in the oxonium ion, \(\mathrm{H_{3}O^{+}}\), is dative, and where do its electrons come from?
cards.a: One O–H bond. A lone pair on the oxygen of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) is donated to an \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) ion.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) has no electrons at all, so it can only bond by accepting a pair.

cards.q: Explain how aluminium chloride forms the dimer \(\mathrm{Al_{2}Cl_{6}}\).
cards.a: Two dative bonds form, each from a chlorine lone pair to the aluminium atom of the other molecule.
marks: In \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\), aluminium has only six electrons in its outer shell, so it is electron-deficient.
A chlorine atom of one \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\) donates a lone pair to the aluminium of a second \(\mathrm{AlCl_{3}}\).
This happens both ways, giving two dative bonds and two chlorine atoms bridging the aluminium atoms.
Each aluminium now has eight outer electrons and four bonds arranged tetrahedrally.

cards.q: The C–C, C=C and C≡C bond lengths are \(0.154\), \(0.134\) and \(0.120\ \text{nm}\). Explain the link between bond length and bond strength.
cards.a: The shorter the bond, the stronger it is: the triple bond is the shortest and strongest.
marks: More shared pairs of electrons between the two nuclei increase the electron density between them.
The nuclei are attracted more strongly to the shared electrons, so they are pulled closer together.
A shorter bond has a stronger electrostatic attraction, so more energy is needed to break it.

cards.q: What is metallic bonding?
cards.a: The strong electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
cards.why: The outer electrons are not attached to any one ion, so they can move through the whole structure.

cards.q: Explain why magnesium (melting point \(650\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)) has a higher melting point than sodium (\(98\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)).
cards.a: Magnesium has stronger metallic bonding.
marks: Each magnesium atom gives two delocalised electrons and forms a \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ion; sodium gives one and forms \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\).
\(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) has a greater charge and a smaller radius than \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\).
So the attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons is stronger, and more energy is needed to overcome it.

cards.q: Explain why metals conduct electricity and are malleable.
cards.a: Delocalised electrons can move; layers of ions can slide without the bonding breaking.
marks: The delocalised electrons are free to move through the lattice and carry charge, in the solid and the liquid.
Metallic bonding is not directional, because the delocalised electrons are shared by all the ions.
So layers of ions can slide over each other when a force is applied, and the bonding holds as they move.

cards.q: Name the four types of crystal structure, with an example of each.
cards.a: Ionic (sodium chloride), metallic (magnesium), giant covalent or macromolecular (diamond, graphite), and simple molecular (iodine, ice).
cards.why: The type of structure, and the bonding in it, decides the melting point, conductivity and solubility.

cards.q: Describe the structure of sodium chloride.
cards.a: A giant ionic lattice. Each \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) ion is surrounded by six \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ions, and each \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ion by six \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\) ions, in a cubic arrangement.
cards.why: Ions of opposite charge alternate in all three directions, so every ion is held by strong attractions to its neighbours.

cards.q: Describe the structure of magnesium.
cards.a: A giant metallic lattice: \(\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}\) ions in a regular arrangement, surrounded by delocalised electrons (two from each atom).
cards.why: The delocalised electrons hold the positive ions together.

cards.q: Describe the structure of diamond and explain its properties.
cards.a: Giant covalent: each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others, arranged tetrahedrally, throughout the structure.
cards.why: Very many strong covalent bonds must break to melt it, so its melting point is very high and it is very hard. There are no delocalised electrons, so it does not conduct.

cards.q: Describe the structure of graphite and use it to explain its properties.
cards.a: Layers of hexagonal rings; each carbon is bonded to three others, with one delocalised electron per atom.
marks: Each carbon atom forms three strong covalent bonds within a flat layer of hexagons.
The fourth outer electron of each carbon is delocalised, so graphite conducts electricity along the layers.
The layers are held together only by weak forces, so they slide over each other: graphite is soft and slippery.
Many strong covalent bonds must break to melt it, so its melting point is very high.

cards.q: What is graphene, and what are its main properties?
cards.a: A single layer of graphite, one atom thick: carbon atoms in hexagons, each bonded to three others.
cards.why: Strong covalent bonds make it very strong for its mass, and its delocalised electrons let it conduct electricity very well.

cards.q: Describe the structure of silicon(IV) oxide, \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\).
cards.a: Giant covalent: each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms, throughout the lattice.
cards.why: Like diamond, it has a very high melting point, is hard, is insoluble in water and does not conduct.

cards.q: Describe the structure of solid iodine and explain why it turns to vapour easily on gentle warming.
cards.a: Simple molecular: \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) molecules held in a regular lattice by London (induced dipole–dipole) forces.
cards.why: Only the weak forces between molecules have to be overcome, not the covalent I–I bonds, so little energy is needed.

cards.q: Describe the structure of ice.
cards.a: Simple molecular: each \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) molecule is hydrogen bonded to four others, arranged tetrahedrally, giving an open lattice.
cards.why: Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs on oxygen, so it can take part in four hydrogen bonds.

cards.q: Explain why diamond has a far higher melting point than iodine, although both contain covalent bonds.
cards.a: Melting diamond breaks covalent bonds; melting iodine only overcomes forces between molecules.
marks: Diamond is giant covalent: melting it means breaking many strong covalent bonds, which needs a lot of energy.
Iodine is simple molecular: melting it only overcomes weak London forces between molecules.
The covalent I–I bonds do not break when iodine melts.

cards.q: Explain the energy changes when a molecular solid melts and then boils.
cards.a: Energy is taken in to overcome the forces between particles, while the temperature stays constant.
marks: Energy supplied during melting or boiling overcomes the attractions between particles, not raising the temperature.
Boiling needs more energy than melting, because the particles must be separated completely.
For a molecular substance only intermolecular forces are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break.

cards.q: True or false: when water boils, the O–H bonds break.
cards.a: False. Boiling overcomes the hydrogen bonds and other forces between water molecules.
cards.why: The bubbles are \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) molecules in the gas phase, not hydrogen and oxygen.

cards.q: Which types of structure conduct electricity, and under what conditions?
cards.a: Metallic: solid and liquid. Ionic: only when molten or dissolved. Simple molecular: not at all. Giant covalent: not at all, except graphite (and graphene).
cards.why: Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move: delocalised electrons or mobile ions.

cards.q: How does solubility in water depend on the type of structure?
cards.a: Many ionic compounds dissolve. Metals and giant covalent substances do not. Simple molecular substances generally do not, unless they can form hydrogen bonds with water.
cards.why: Water dissolves a substance when the attractions it can form to the particles compensate for the forces broken.

cards.q: Substance A melts at \(1610\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), is insoluble in water, and does not conduct electricity as a solid or when molten. Deduce its structure.
cards.a: Giant covalent (macromolecular).
steps: Very high melting point: strong bonds throughout the structure, so not simple molecular.
No conduction even when molten: no mobile ions, so not ionic; no delocalised electrons, so not metallic.
So it is giant covalent, like \(\mathrm{SiO_{2}}\).
cards.why: Combine all the clues: one property alone rarely decides the structure.

cards.q: Substance B melts at \(714\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), dissolves in water, and conducts electricity only when molten or dissolved. Deduce its structure.
cards.a: Giant ionic lattice.
steps: High melting point: strong forces throughout the structure.
Does not conduct as a solid but does when molten or dissolved: ions that are fixed in the solid become free to move.
So it is ionic.
cards.why: A metal would conduct as a solid as well; a giant covalent substance would not conduct at all.

cards.q: Outline simple tests to find the type of structure of an unknown white solid.
cards.a: Test how easily it melts, whether it dissolves in water, and whether it conducts as a solid, when molten and in solution.
marks: Heat a small sample: melting easily suggests a simple molecular structure.
Add to water: many ionic solids dissolve; giant covalent solids do not.
Test conductivity of the solid with a simple circuit: conducting suggests a metal (or graphite).
Test conductivity of the solution or melt: conducting then, but not as a solid, suggests ionic.

cards.q: Explain what decides the shape of a simple molecule or ion.
cards.a: The number of electron pairs around the central atom, and how many of them are lone pairs.
marks: Electron pairs (bonding pairs and lone pairs) in the outer shell of the central atom repel each other.
They arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimise repulsion.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, which changes the bond angles.

cards.q: Put the three types of electron-pair repulsion in order, and say how lone pairs affect bond angles.
cards.a: Lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
cards.why: Each lone pair squeezes the bonding pairs closer together, reducing the bond angle by about \(2.5^{\circ}\) per lone pair from \(109.5^{\circ}\).

cards.q: Describe how to work out the number of bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom, using ammonia as the example.
cards.a: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around nitrogen.
steps: Count the outer electrons of the central atom: N has 5.
Add one electron for each atom bonded by a single bond (here 3 H): 5 + 3 = 8. For an ion, add one electron per negative charge or subtract one per positive charge.
Divide by 2 for the number of electron pairs: 4.
Bonding pairs = number of bonded atoms = 3, so lone pairs = 4 − 3 = 1.
cards.why: Four pairs give a tetrahedral arrangement; with one lone pair the shape is trigonal pyramidal.

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{BeCl_{2}}\).
cards.a: Linear, \(180^{\circ}\). Two bonding pairs, no lone pairs.
cards.why: Two electron pairs are furthest apart on opposite sides of the central atom.

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{BCl_{3}}\).
cards.a: Trigonal planar, \(120^{\circ}\). Three bonding pairs, no lone pairs.
cards.why: Boron has only three outer electrons, so it forms three bonds and has no lone pair.

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{CH_{4}}\) and of the ammonium ion, \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\).
cards.a: Both tetrahedral, \(109.5^{\circ}\). Four bonding pairs, no lone pairs.
cards.why: They are isoelectronic: \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\) also has four bonding pairs around the central atom.

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\).
cards.a: Trigonal pyramidal, \(107^{\circ}\). Three bonding pairs, one lone pair.
cards.why: The lone pair repels more than the bonding pairs, closing the angle from \(109.5^{\circ}\).

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\).
cards.a: Bent (V-shaped, non-linear), \(104.5^{\circ}\). Two bonding pairs, two lone pairs.
cards.why: Two lone pairs repel even more strongly, so the angle is smaller than in \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\).

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\).
cards.a: Linear, \(180^{\circ}\). Two double bonds, no lone pairs on carbon.
cards.why: A double bond counts as one region of electron density when working out the shape.

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angles of \(\mathrm{PCl_{5}}\) (gas).
cards.a: Trigonal bipyramidal, \(120^{\circ}\) and \(90^{\circ}\). Five bonding pairs, no lone pairs.
cards.why: Three Cl atoms lie in a plane at \(120^{\circ}\); the other two are above and below, at \(90^{\circ}\) to that plane.

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{SF_{6}}\).
cards.a: Octahedral, \(90^{\circ}\). Six bonding pairs, no lone pairs.
cards.why: Sulfur can expand its outer shell beyond eight electrons because it is in Period 3.

cards.q: Explain why the bond angles in \(\mathrm{CH_{4}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) are \(109.5^{\circ}\), \(107^{\circ}\) and \(104.5^{\circ}\).
cards.a: Each has four electron pairs, but the number of lone pairs increases from 0 to 2.
marks: All three have four electron pairs around the central atom, arranged tetrahedrally.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs.
\(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) has one lone pair and \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) two, so the bonding pairs are pushed closer together and the angle gets smaller.

cards.q: Predict the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{XeF_{4}}\). (Xe has 8 outer electrons.)
cards.a: Square planar, \(90^{\circ}\). Four bonding pairs, two lone pairs.
steps: Electrons around Xe: \(8 + 4 = 12\), so 6 pairs.
Four F atoms, so 4 bonding pairs and \(6 - 4 = 2\) lone pairs.
Six pairs point to the corners of an octahedron; the two lone pairs sit opposite each other to be as far apart as possible.
The four F atoms are left in a square plane at \(90^{\circ}\).
cards.why: Lone pairs take positions that keep the lone pair–lone pair repulsion as small as possible.

cards.q: Predict the shape and bond angle of the \(\mathrm{AlCl_{4}^{-}}\) ion.
cards.a: Tetrahedral, \(109.5^{\circ}\).
steps: Al has 3 outer electrons; add 4 for four Cl atoms and 1 for the negative charge: \(3 + 4 + 1 = 8\).
That is 4 pairs, all bonding (four Cl atoms), with no lone pairs.
cards.why: It has the same electron arrangement as \(\mathrm{CH_{4}}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\).

cards.q: Predict the shape and bond angle of \(\mathrm{PF_{6}^{-}}\).
cards.a: Octahedral, \(90^{\circ}\).
steps: P has 5 outer electrons; add 6 for six F atoms and 1 for the charge: \(5 + 6 + 1 = 12\).
That is 6 pairs, all bonding, with no lone pairs.
cards.why: It is analogous to \(\mathrm{SF_{6}}\).

cards.q: Predict the shape and bond angle of the \(\mathrm{NH_{2}^{-}}\) ion.
cards.a: Bent (V-shaped), about \(104.5^{\circ}\).
steps: N has 5 outer electrons; add 2 for two H atoms and 1 for the charge: \(5 + 2 + 1 = 8\), so 4 pairs.
Two bonding pairs and \(4 - 2 = 2\) lone pairs.
cards.why: It has the same arrangement of pairs as \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: Give the shape and bond angles around each carbon atom in ethene, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{4}}\).
cards.a: Trigonal planar, \(120^{\circ}\), around each carbon.
cards.why: Each carbon has three regions of electron density (two C–H bonds and the C=C double bond) and no lone pairs.

cards.q: Define electronegativity.
cards.a: The power (ability) of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
cards.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element. Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group.

cards.q: Explain why the H–Cl bond is polar, and show its partial charges.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{H^{\delta+}{-}Cl^{\delta-}}\): chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen.
marks: Chlorine attracts the bonding pair of electrons more strongly than hydrogen does.
The electron distribution in the bond is unsymmetrical, closer to chlorine.
Chlorine gains a partial negative charge, δ−, and hydrogen a partial positive charge, δ+.

cards.q: Explain why ionic and covalent bonding are described as the two extremes of a continuum.
cards.a: As the electronegativity difference between two atoms increases, the bond becomes more polar, until the electron pair is effectively transferred and the bond is ionic.
cards.why: Two identical atoms (as in \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\)) give a pure covalent bond; most real bonds lie somewhere between the extremes.

cards.q: Explain why \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) has polar bonds but no permanent dipole.
cards.a: The molecule is symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel.
marks: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so each C=O bond is polar.
The molecule is linear, with the two bond dipoles pointing in opposite directions at \(180^{\circ}\).
The dipoles cancel, so the molecule has no overall (permanent) dipole.

cards.q: Which is a polar molecule: \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) or \(\mathrm{CHCl_{3}}\)? Explain.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CHCl_{3}}\) is polar; \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) is not.
cards.why: In tetrahedral \(\mathrm{CCl_{4}}\) four identical C–Cl dipoles cancel. In \(\mathrm{CHCl_{3}}\) one C–H replaces a C–Cl, so the dipoles no longer cancel.

cards.q: Predict whether \(\mathrm{BF_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{NF_{3}}\) are polar molecules.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{BF_{3}}\) is non-polar; \(\mathrm{NF_{3}}\) is polar.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{BF_{3}}\) is trigonal planar, so the three B–F dipoles cancel. \(\mathrm{NF_{3}}\) is trigonal pyramidal, so its N–F dipoles do not cancel.

cards.q: A charged rod is held next to thin streams of water and of hexane running from burettes. What happens, and why?
cards.a: The water stream is deflected towards the rod; the hexane stream is not.
cards.why: Water molecules are polar and turn so that their oppositely charged end faces the rod. Hexane molecules have no permanent dipole.

cards.q: Explain how induced dipole–dipole (London) forces arise between molecules.
cards.a: Temporary dipoles induce dipoles in neighbouring molecules, and the two attract.
marks: Electrons are constantly moving, so at any instant their distribution in a molecule may be uneven: an instantaneous (temporary) dipole.
This dipole induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule.
The two dipoles attract each other. These forces act between all molecules.

cards.q: What makes London forces between molecules stronger?
cards.a: More electrons in the molecule, and a larger area of contact between molecules.
cards.why: More electrons give larger temporary dipoles; a long, unbranched shape lets molecules get closer along more of their length.

cards.q: Explain how permanent dipole–dipole forces arise, using hydrogen chloride as an example.
cards.a: The \(\delta+\) H of one HCl molecule attracts the \(\delta-\) Cl of a neighbouring molecule.
marks: HCl has a polar bond and is not symmetrical, so it has a permanent dipole.
The partial positive end of one molecule attracts the partial negative end of another.
These act in addition to the London forces between the molecules.

cards.q: What conditions are needed for hydrogen bonding between molecules?
cards.a: H bonded to N, O or F in one molecule, and a lone pair on N, O or F in another.
marks: A hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a very electronegative atom: nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
This makes the hydrogen strongly δ+ (it is a small atom with no inner electrons to shield its nucleus).
It is attracted to a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of a neighbouring molecule.

cards.q: Describe the hydrogen bonding between two water molecules.
cards.a: The \(\delta+\) H of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the \(\delta-\) O of another. The O–H···O atoms lie in a straight line (about \(180^{\circ}\)).
cards.why: Hydrogen bonds are drawn as dashed lines from the hydrogen to the lone pair.

cards.q: Describe the hydrogen bonding in liquid \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) and in liquid \(\mathrm{HF}\).
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\): the \(\delta+\) H of one molecule is attracted to the lone pair on the N of another (N–H···N).
\(\mathrm{HF}\): the \(\delta+\) H is attracted to a lone pair on the F of another molecule (F–H···F).
cards.why: The hydrogen bond is strongest with fluorine, the most electronegative atom.

cards.q: Which of these form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}OCH_{3}}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}F}\), \(\mathrm{CH_{3}NH_{2}}\)?
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}OH}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}NH_{2}}\) only.
steps: Look for an H atom bonded directly to N, O or F.
Ethanol has an O–H bond and methylamine has N–H bonds: both hydrogen bond.
In \(\mathrm{CH_{3}OCH_{3}}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_{3}F}\) every H is bonded to carbon, so they cannot hydrogen bond with each other.
cards.why: Having an O or F atom is not enough: the hydrogen must be on the N, O or F.

cards.q: Explain why water (boiling point \(100\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)) boils at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulfide (\(-60\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)), even though \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\) has more electrons.
cards.a: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds; \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\) molecules cannot.
marks: Oxygen is very electronegative, so there are hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
Sulfur is not electronegative enough, so H₂S has only weaker permanent dipole–dipole and London forces.
Hydrogen bonds are the strongest intermolecular force, so more energy is needed to separate water molecules.

cards.q: Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water.
cards.a: Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in ice in an open lattice, further apart than in the liquid.
marks: In ice each water molecule is hydrogen bonded to four others in a regular tetrahedral arrangement.
The hydrogen bonds are relatively long, so this open lattice holds the molecules further apart than in liquid water.
When ice melts some hydrogen bonds break, the lattice collapses and the molecules move closer together.

cards.q: Explain why the boiling points of the straight-chain alkanes increase with chain length.
cards.a: Longer chains have more electrons and more surface contact, so stronger London forces.
marks: Alkanes are non-polar, so the only intermolecular forces are London forces.
Each extra CH₂ adds more electrons and lengthens the molecule, increasing the area of contact.
London forces get stronger, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

cards.q: Pentane boils at \(36\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) and its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane at \(10\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). Explain the difference.
cards.a: Branching reduces the contact between molecules, weakening the London forces.
marks: Both have the same formula, so the same number of electrons.
The branched molecule is more compact (nearly spherical), so molecules cannot pack as closely and have a smaller area of contact.
London forces are weaker, so less energy is needed to separate the molecules.

cards.q: Ethanol (26 electrons) boils at \(78\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\); propane (26 electrons) boils at \(-42\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). Explain the difference.
cards.a: Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds; propane molecules do not.
marks: With the same number of electrons, the London forces are similar.
Ethanol has an O–H group, so there are also hydrogen bonds between its molecules.
Extra energy is needed to break the hydrogen bonds, so ethanol is less volatile.

cards.q: Boiling points: HF \(20\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), HCl \(-85\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), HBr \(-67\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), HI \(-35\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). Explain the trend.
cards.a: From HCl to HI London forces increase; HF is anomalous because of hydrogen bonding.
marks: From HCl to HI the number of electrons increases, so London forces get stronger.
The bonds become less polar from HCl to HI, so permanent dipole–dipole forces get weaker, but the increase in London forces is bigger.
HF has hydrogen bonds between molecules, which are much stronger, so it has the highest boiling point.

cards.q: True or false: permanent dipole–dipole forces are always stronger than London forces.
cards.a: False. London forces can be the larger contribution.
cards.why: HI boils higher than HCl although its bond is less polar: its many more electrons give much stronger London forces.

cards.q: True or false: a hydrogen bond is the covalent bond between a hydrogen atom and an oxygen atom in a water molecule.
cards.a: False. The O–H bond is covalent. A hydrogen bond is a force between molecules.
cards.why: It is the attraction between a δ+ H on one molecule and a lone pair on N, O or F in another.

cards.q: Explain how water dissolves an ionic compound such as sodium chloride.
cards.a: Polar water molecules surround and attract the ions: the ions are hydrated.
marks: The δ− oxygen atoms of water molecules are attracted to the positive ions.
The δ+ hydrogen atoms of water molecules are attracted to the negative ions.
The energy released when the ions are hydrated helps to overcome the attraction between ions in the lattice.

cards.q: Explain why ethanol mixes completely with water, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
cards.a: The O–H group forms hydrogen bonds with water; a long hydrocarbon chain cannot.
marks: The O–H group of an alcohol forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
In ethanol the hydrocarbon part is small, so this outweighs it.
In hexan-1-ol the long non-polar chain cannot hydrogen bond, and it disrupts the hydrogen bonding between water molecules, so solubility is low.

cards.q: Explain why halogenoalkanes, although polar, are almost insoluble in water.
cards.a: They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
marks: Water molecules are held together by strong hydrogen bonds.
A halogenoalkane cannot form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
The attractions it could form with water are weaker than the hydrogen bonds that would have to break, so it does not dissolve.

cards.q: Iodine is almost insoluble in water but dissolves well in hexane. Why?
cards.a: Non-aqueous solvents dissolve substances with similar intermolecular forces: iodine and hexane are both held by London forces.
cards.why: The London forces between \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) and hexane molecules replace those broken, whereas iodine cannot replace water’s hydrogen bonds.
